title: Christmas trees: How early is too early to buy one and will it last until Christmas?
description: The appropriate time to put up your Christmas tree is a question almost as divisive as whether Yorkshire pudding has a place on the Christmas dinner p
body: The appropriate time to put up your Christmas tree is a question almost as divisive as whether Yorkshire pudding has a place on the Christmas dinner plate. Some might feel the best time is just after Bonfire Night, others may think Christmas Eve is more apt, and most will probably plump for somewhere in between. Tesco started selling Christmas trees at half-price this week and said more than 90% of its trees had sold out by the end of November last year.Lidl and some other retailers are also launching their ranges next week, while others including Dobbies Garden Centres are waiting until the last week of November.But with Christmas Day still six weeks away, is it unwise to rush into buying a real tree so early? And do you risk spending your Christmas week cleaning up piles of pine needles?Probably, says Mick Walker, from Bolton Christmas Trees, which grows trees in the Scottish Highlands before sending them to homes across the UK."It might last until the beginning of Christmas, but it won't last the full holiday," he warns. "Unless its a potted one, it's going to be sagging by Christmas Day - big time."He calls Tesco's half-price deal "insane", adding that it's "sucking them into buying something now that isn't going to do the job". So when would he suggest is the best time? "If it was me, I'd put it up a week before Christmas eve, [and it will] last straight through until New Year."The most popular Christmas trees available in the UK are the Nordmann fir variety, which are non-drop, meaning they don't drop their needles. Norway Spruce is another common variety and have a strong pine scent, but generally should be kept outdoors or put up just before Christmas.Pine trees, Walker says, have the longest lifespan, but he concedes they lack that classic Christmas look.Or, of course, you could opt for a tried-and-tested artificial tree, which is what Katie McDonald from Belfast put up in her house last week."When I was a kid my mum always waited to the last minute to let us kids put the tree up. We would be the last house on our street and the last of all our friends to get the tree up," she tells the BBC."So I made myself a wee childlike promise that when I had my own house I'd be one of the first to put my tree up."She says she will replace her artificial tree with a real one in a few weeks, so it is in prime condition come Christmas Day.

schema.headline: Christmas trees: How early is too early to buy one and will it last until Christmas?

title: King Charles jokes with Elton John as he marks 78th birthday with radio show
description: King Charles and Sir Elton John joked about the problems of ageing as the pair joined for a special radio show to coincide with the monarch's 78th bir
body: King Charles and Sir Elton John joked about the problems of ageing as the pair joined for a special radio show to coincide with the monarch's 78th birthday.Sir Elton, 79, was joined on his regular Rocket Hour radio show for a special episode during which the King shared his musical memories as the pair chose 14 songs together.The programme also marked the 50th anniversary of the King's Trust and highlighted how musicians have supported the charity's efforts. "We and the Trust are definitely still standing," the King said, as he highlighted Sir Elton's track I'm Still Standing as one of his favourites because of the song's "message of resilience".The music legend joked in reply: "I'm still sitting now, though" giving a large laugh, with the King chuckling: "With occasional bits dropping off here and there. I know this is a terrible problem as we get older."The special was recorded last month at Apple Music Studios in south London and premiered on Saturday morning.The King recalled Sir Elton's 1986 performance at Wembley Arena, which marked the charity's 10th anniversary."I suspect that no-one who was present on that night in 1986 could possibly forget your performance of I'm Still Standing," King Charles said."I know people in all kinds of circumstances find this song inspiring, not only for its marvellous spirit, but also its message of resilience. And certainly, 40 years on from that remarkable concert, we and the Trust are definitely still standing."The pair selected a total of 14 tracks. King Charles picked Giant by Calvin Harris and Rag'n'Bone Man, telling Sir Elton that the song summed up his charity because of its message of finding strength from others.Also selected was Bob Dylan's Gotta Serve Somebody, Muse's Feeling Good and Nectar Woode's Wine into Water, which features Sir Elton on piano.The Rocket Man star asked the King to highlight a song that he found "extremely meaningful". Replying that there is "nothing more meaningful than love", the King described an "unforgettable performance" of The Beatles' 1967 hit All You Need is Love by Sir Paul McCartney in 2002 at a concert in honour of Queen Elizabeth II's Golden Jubilee."I shall never forget the magic of witnessing a simply unforgettable performance of All You Need Is Love for my late mother's Golden Jubilee at the Party At The Palace concert with Paul McCartney, Rod Stewart and Joe Cocker, and I think with Phil Collins on drums, Brian May and Eric Clapton on guitar and an all-star backing choir," the King said."It really is a totally timeless song with a timeless message."

schema.headline: King Charles jokes with Elton John as he marks 78th birthday with radio show

title: Body found on French beach after attempted Channel crossing
description: The coastguard described the boarding process of the makeshift vessel as "chaotic", adding that five men were attended to by firefighters at the scene
body: The coastguard described the boarding process of the makeshift vessel as "chaotic", adding that five men were attended to by firefighters at the scene for signs of hypothermia. A small craft was then deployed which - along with "land-based units" from the local fire and rescue service - conducted "a thorough sweep of the area but found no one in the water"."Following the operation, at approximately 08:00 (09:00 GMT) the body of a man in his twenties was discovered on the beach," the coastguard reported. It adds an investigation will be opened to "determine the circumstances surrounding the incident".In the latest week of data, ending 8 November, the UK government reported that 903 migrants arrived by small boat into the UK in 14 boats. A further 624 migrants were prevented from making the crossing, the data shows. Earlier this year, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood ordered an urgent review after two boats carrying 21 people landed in Kent without being intercepted. "Our improved monitoring has led to uncontrolled crossings becoming incredibly rare, but even one is one too many," she said at the time.

schema.headline: Body found on French beach after attempted Channel crossing

title: Russell Brand, David Walliams and Married at First Sight: Is this a reckoning for TV?
description: This week, the dark side of television has come crashing into the open.On Monday, disgraced entertainer Russell Brand was jailed for rape and sexual a
body: This week, the dark side of television has come crashing into the open.On Monday, disgraced entertainer Russell Brand was jailed for rape and sexual assault.Twenty-four hours later, author and comedian David Walliams was unmasked and accused of preying on young women. By Friday the Metropolitan Police had launched an investigation into further allegations about him.Also in the last week, Married at First Sight UK has been cancelled following allegations of rape on the hit TV show.These are all very different stories, but each can be seen as a major reckoning with abuse of power and culture in the industry.So why is this all happening now?In reality, the glut of recent days is something of a coincidence.All these revelations began with journalistic investigations that started years ago.From my own experience - including in my Panorama on Married at First Sight UK - I know investigations typically take a very long time to reach a conclusion, from initial tip-off, to evidence-gathering, corroboration, getting responses, and eventually reporting."The truth is, these stories have a long build up. It can be incredibly difficult to get [them] in the papers," Sunday Times columnist Hadley Freeman told me.In the case of Brand, there was then a police investigation too, before an outcome was reached in court.Together these stories represent the consequences of changes that began years ago, rather than a sudden cultural shift in the entertainment industry.It should also be said that Walliams denies the allegations against him. The men accused of rape and sexual misconduct on MAFS UK have also denied all the allegations.What has changed is that women (because it almost always is women) have seen others speaking up - which, according to broadcaster Kirsty Wark, has given them "courage to do the same". She describes those who have come forward as "beyond brave".When looking at what’s driving more women to speak up, much can be traced back to the revelations about Harvey Weinstein and the #MeToo movement.It changed the perception of whether victims would be believed.In the past, women alleging this sort of behaviour faced barriers - being seen as opportunistic, fearing retaliation, believing they might be the only one.Now, there can be a snowball effect. Once one, two or three come forward, that prompts others to revisit their experiences - which they may have dismissed or subdued."There is more of a sense that you will now be listened to," said Freeman.It's also clear that when women see action taken, it can encourage others to speak up as well - as it helps counter the widely-held assumption that reporting abuse results in nothing.When another high-profile man, MasterChef presenter Gregg Wallace, faced accusations of a very different and much lesser order, relating mostly to inappropriate sexual language and humour, the reaction was similar.Last summer, an independent inquiry upheld dozens of claims against him, and he was sacked. Wallace said "none of the serious allegations" against him had been upheld but that he was "deeply sorry for any distress caused".One young woman I spoke to in my investigation into Wallace texted me at the time, to give her reaction to his sacking."I really believe this will encourage young girls going into the TV industry to have the courage to speak up, if they feel something is wrong," she told me.But unions say it is still difficult for junior freelance workers, who often find their income unstable and unpredictable, to speak up.Vulnerable workers "continue to fear raising concerns", said head of broadcast union Bectu, Philippa Childs.She's echoed by Freeman, who said an "attitude of protecting the talent" remained."There will always be wealthy famous predators," she said. But, she added: "Hopefully more and more people at TV stations and movie studios are willing to hear these young people and will take them seriously”.For more senior people in TV, raising the alarm can also be difficult.Earlier this week, comedian Lucy Beaumont told Sky News: "The reason high-profile people are not saying anything is because they lose work, because you're seen that you might be a trouble causer. It does need to be said that there needs to be some intervention."Social media has also played a role in encouraging people to speak up.And policing investigations have had to keep pace - and adapt - with media scrutiny often prompting authorities to investigate.Attitudes towards women who speak up are also starting to change – although not always.Some of what unfolded in court during the Russell Brand case felt like a throwback to how rape cases used to be conducted.Many have commented on Brand's lawyer's defence tactics against the accusers on the stand - behaviour Freeman said would have been "standard" in the past.But Freeman noted it was heartening to hear the judge’s remarks in summing up the case - which have also been widely shared by women online and praised for dispelling rape myths.When Mr Justice Bennathan sentenced Brand to ten-and-a-half years, he told him: "Whatever women wear, wherever they go, indeed whatever they drink, they retain the right to say no.""I think attitudes have changed,” said Freeman. “It doesn't mean those assaults don't happen any more but attitudes around them have changed.”This week, comedian Deborah Frances-White told BBC Radio 4's The World at One that young women were "definitely" still being exploited in the comedy industry.And in the past few days, I've had tip-offs about other celebrities allegedly abusing their power. No doubt other journalists have too.None of those is reportable, yet. As Freeman said: "There are other names out there, but you and I couldn't name them as we'd be sued".But one "cheering thing", she said, was that the sort of jokes and innuendos from the nineties and noughties, or even the optics of seeing a much older man with a younger girl would no longer be "glossed over"."It wouldn't be laughed at, and it wouldn't be 'nudge nudge'," Freeman said. "That kind of open, in your face, weirdness won't happen any more"."On the downside, that may make it harder to identify predators, if it means these things are kept more in the shadows."Then there’s the use of gagging orders and other legal routes often used by celebrities and media organisations to stop women speaking out.Last week, a High Court judge rejected an injunction request by Walliams, clearing the way for him to be named."There are lots of barriers to speaking out, and those that have access to wealth or fame will often use legal measures to deter alleged victims from doing so," Harriet Wistrich, from the Centre for Women's Justice, told me.That too, may be starting to change.This week, multiple government ministers have spoken against non-disclosure agreements and called for further restrictions on their use.Change could come in other areas too.Next week, Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy will convene industry leaders to urge them to improve safeguarding practices - while Channel 4 bosses are due to appear in front an MPs on Tuesday.When MAFS UK was cancelled, Channel 4 said the programme had "run its course" and apologised to the women involved in the investigation.It said the review found that in Channel 4 and production company CPL's handling of the issues raised at the time, there was no breach of Ofcom's broadcasting code.There is growing recognition that those at the top of media organisations have a responsibility to root out abuse. It can't just be down to the victims."People in positions of power have a duty to speak up too," said Wark."Broadcasters, production companies and those financing productions all have a responsibility to ensure protections are upheld," added Josephine Brassey, from Women in Film and TV, while Philippa Childs urged the creative industries to accept that their current internal reporting mechanisms were "inadequate".What everyone seems to agree on is that this can't be another empty tipping point with no real, lasting change.Maybe this time it could really be a watershed moment.If you have more information about this story, you can reach Noor by email at noor.nanji@bbc.co.uk

schema.headline: Russell Brand, David Walliams and Married at First Sight: Is this a reckoning for TV?

title: WSL: Chelsea 1-0 Man City - Sonia Bompastor's risks pay off
description: In any big encounter you will often hear managers say it is the "fine margins" that decide a game of football.Sometimes it is luck. Sometimes it is in
body: In any big encounter you will often hear managers say it is the "fine margins" that decide a game of football.Sometimes it is luck. Sometimes it is individual brilliance. But on Saturday it was Sonia Bompastor's bold decisions that helped Chelsea beat Manchester City 1-0.The top-of-the-table Women's Super League clash was as intriguing as you would hope it to be and both managers needed to be on their toes.Chelsea boss Bompastor "took responsibility" and brought off struggling defender Kadeisha Buchanan 12 minutes in, and it had the desired effect.City striker Khadija Shaw was not able to get in behind like she had done in the early stages, and Buchanan's replacement Veerle Buurman shone.Was it a tactical substitution or was Buchanan injured?When the fourth official's board went up showing the number of the player Buurman would replace, there was confusion from Chelsea players.It was clearly not planned, nor had Buchanan asked to come off. There was no apparent injury as she jogged off and she was clearly upset, heading straight down the tunnel.Asked to clarify the situation, Bompastor said: "Yesterday in training she got a knock to her head in contact with a team-mate but she was fine."She was fine in the evening and we assessed her again this morning and everything was fine. I had that information before the game. "But I felt from watching her at the beginning of the game that she was not herself. I took the responsibility to make the substitution."I felt I was almost forced to do that. I know my player and she was not in the game."Whether Buchanan's shaky start was down to that knock is unclear, but Bompastor knew her decision was a risk and was willing to act immediately.Buurman instantly marshalled Shaw, and City's early threat was quietened as Chelsea regained control and ended the half a goal up thanks to Sandy Baltimore.Shaw did not record a shot on target and in-form England international Lauren Hemp was quiet as Buurman performed well in a stubborn Chelsea backline.City manager Andree Jeglertz said he did not think the switch "changed the picture", but he was outsmarted by Bompastor during the 90 minutes.Bompastor admitted she had not spoken properly with Buchanan at full-time but promised to "explain myself to her". "I just told her a few words. My assistant coach Camille Abily will have done that already probably and I think everything will be fine," said the Frenchwoman."I always have good relationships with the players, bring them clarity, and I'm always direct and honest so they have the information. It won't be any different."The risky substitution was compounded by an injury to striker Melvine Malard 23 minutes later, meaning Chelsea's XI was tweaked twice before half-time.Not normally one to bring on players at the break, Bompastor was smart and hooked goalscorer Baltimore, who was likely still buzzing from her impact.She was replaced by Maika Hamano, who went on to play the ball through to Alyssa Thompson when she was brought down by City goalkeeper Ayaka Yamashita, and she was shown a straight red card as a result, ending the visitors' comeback hopes."We knew going into the second half we only had one substitution slot and we knew Sandy has been playing lots of minutes," said Bompastor."I knew she probably didn't have the legs to go more than maybe 60 minutes and I knew I didn't have more slots after that. I was forced into this one as well. "It paid off and that's good. Sandy was doing well but she knows the reason why we made that decision. "That's the first time I experienced that kind of substitution in the first half. It's good for my own experience."Bompastor's bravery was rewarded and, while City certainly had their chances, Chelsea defended resiliently to see out the narrow win.Jeglertz could not find a solution to Chelsea's attacking threats, which came largely from wide areas via Ellie Carpenter and Thompson.Vivianne Miedema returned from injury and looked sharp when she came on for City in the second half, but it was not enough to change the result.In contrast, Bompastor's risks proved the difference, and they were made with former Chelsea boss Emma Hayes, who mastered the art of bullish decisions, watching on in the stands alongside Sarina Wiegman at Stamford Bridge.Chelsea's victory bumped them back up to the WSL summit, a point above City, while Buurman picked up the player-of-the-match award."It paid off today. You have to be brave to make that decision in that moment because you know bringing in a player in the game is a risk," said Bompastor. "We had a good conversation with Veerle and she was clear on why she wasn't starting the game. That clarity was important for when she came in. "She had a really good performance against a top player. Sometimes when it doesn't work, it's not so positive, but today it was."You have to react and be the one that analyses the situation and make decisions. I'm used to it, even if you don't see lots of substitutions in the first half most of the time in football."

schema.headline: WSL: Chelsea 1-0 Man City - Sonia Bompastor's risks pay off

title: Even Grand Theft Auto's original creators haven't been able to play GTA 6
description: Image source, Rockstar Games / Take-Two InteractiveImage caption, GTA 6 will feature brand new protagonists Jason and Lucia - the first playable femal
body: Image source, Rockstar Games / Take-Two InteractiveImage caption, GTA 6 will feature brand new protagonists Jason and Lucia - the first playable female character in any of the 3D gamesByLaura CressTechnology reporterAfter a 13-year wait, two delays, and several high-profile leaks, the launch of Grand Theft Auto 6 is fast approaching.The next chapter in the nearly 30-year-old series, where players explore open worlds and break the law, has created an extraordinary level of anticipation.And with developer Rockstar Games keeping their biggest release yet, tightly under wraps, even the people who helped bring the original to life aren't getting special treatment."We're all waiting to see what they've done," Dave Jones, GTA's co-creator, tells me, sitting alongside the original game's writer and publicist, Brian Baglow.Have either of them been able to play the new game ahead of launch?Baglow shakes his head. He's not complaining, though. "I've got the pre-order," he says.Image caption, Brian Baglow (left) and Dave Jones, worked on the original Grand Theft AutoThe original Grand Theft Auto was released in 1997 in Dundee, Scotland by DMA Design, a relatively small team, at least judging by later games' standards.Following its success with puzzle game Lemmings, the studio was toying around with the idea of making a racing game, initially called Race'n'Chase.Sitting in the state-of-the-art computer lab at Dundee's Abertay University decades on, Jones tells me the developers still felt they had to bring something new to the table."At DMA, we always wanted to do something different," he says. "What was the unique spin we could put on it?"Part of the answer, he said, came in what feels like a premise gamers take for granted now - "just getting out of the car".He says the idea of being able to not only drive but switch and steal cars, running about on foot as you did so, meant "all of a sudden you had this interesting mix of gaming coming together".Image gallerySkip image galleryImage source, DMA Design / BMG InteractiveImage caption, The original Grand Theft Auto came out in 1997 and featured a top-down view in 2DSlide 1 of 7, A screenshot from the original Grand Theft Auto. The words BUSTED! is shown in yellow. A top down view shows several police cars with sirens on and a red car with door open, and a person on the road., The original Grand Theft Auto came out in 1997 and featured a top-down view in 2D'More fun' playing the bad guyThe team envisioned a game, Jones says, where you could play as both a criminal and a police officer. But he quickly reconsidered the second option, as it would require players to behave "by the book"."At some point we just said, you know what, it's way more fun playing the bad guy, so that's what the game was about," he adds.Despite some of these novel approaches to the game's design, Jones says it was a "slow burn" in sales compared with Lemmings - partly because you had to "play it to get it"."For the whole of the year that GTA came out, it just kept going and selling and selling," says Baglow."And we reckoned it was the word of mouth. The people who had played it going, oh my God, have you played this game?"Its themes of criminality and violence sparked controversy - leading to debates in the UK Parliament and calls to ban the game. Yet it later transpired much of that  was generated by the game's own publisher, BMG Interactive, as a viral marketing stunt."We just did things that we felt were fun," says Jones. "We never at any point kind of thought, should we do that? Is it controversial? We never thought that way."Although relatively basic in appearance, with its top-down 2D view and more arcade-like graphics, the original game forged the blueprint for the series' signature satire still seen in much later, more advanced GTAs today.Despite being set in an exaggerated version of American cities, its Scottishness could still be found in its humour and its outsider perspective, says Guardian video games editor Keza MacDonald."It's a deeply satirical game," she says. "It really takes aim at the hyper-individualist, hyper-capitalist nature of the US."Partly out of necessity due to their comparatively low budget and the cost of real-world licenses, the team came up with cheeky brand names and fake radio stations players could listen to while driving around and causing mayhem.Though some of these choices were made out of limitations, Baglow says the world-building is the element he's most proud of from the original, which is still a big part of what makes a title feel like GTA."It's the business names, it's the radio stations, it's the lyrics, it's the DJs," he says."Every part of that is making you believe that this environment you're in is a big cohesive whole."Image source, Rockstar Games / Take-Two InteractiveImage caption, The new game's location - the fictional state of Leonida - is expected to be double the size of GTA V's mapWhen GTA V launched in 2013, it made $1bn (£760m) in just three days - faster than any entertainment product had achieved at the time.The series evolved into a cultural reference point itself - something people recognised, understood and even referenced outside gaming."I've seen movies where someone says 'don't go all GTA on me'... it was just surreal," says Jones.MacDonald, joining me in Glasgow's gaming cafe, RCade, tells me there's an argument now that while earlier GTAs "took a lot" from the big screen, films are now "probably more influenced by GTA" than the other way round.She says later titles in the series have a cinematic feel, but also reflect the distinct identity it has forged for itself.As for why Jones believes the game has become such a cultural phenomenon, he says it's the simple fact that it's "based on real life"."It's not like a lot of games like sci-fi or adventure or fantasy," he says. "There's nothing you have to learn about it, as long as you know a city and driving."Image caption, "It means so much to so many people," says Baglow, leftGTA 6 is expected to surpass its predecessor on every level, not only in scale and scope, but also in revenue.Already, both PlayStation and Xbox, the two platforms the game is initially releasing on, have said the game has become the most pre-ordered title in their digital stores' history.This may be partly down to its huge size (212GB), meaning many are pre-ordering to "pre-load" the game, ready to play it immediately at launch rather than waiting to download it.The hype has spilt into the real world, with London's Selfridges transformed into a Vice City-themed pop-up attraction and fictional GTA brands appearing on billboards across Miami, the city that inspired the game."Everyone is extremely excited for this," says MacDonald. "It's hoping to be a shot in the arm for the general games industry, but also every player is looking to see what Rockstar's been doing for all this time."It's very rare that we have this one massive game that everybody's going to be, if not playing, then certainly interested in."Do Jones and Baglow ever wish they were still working on the game now, given the huge amount of global attention focused on it?"I think everybody loves having their time on it, for one, two, three versions," Jones says."But eventually you want to go off and do other things as well."Baglow adds that watching "the rest of the world fall in love with the game over the last 29 years has just been joyful"."It means so much to so many people - it's been fantastic."Get in touchAre you a fan of the game? Get in touch.

schema.headline: Even Grand Theft Auto's original creators haven't been able to play GTA 6

title: I took Vinted to court to get my money back
description: Mali Osmelak never imagined that selling clothes on Vinted would end with a court claim to recover almost £6,000.She started trading on the platform t
body: Mali Osmelak never imagined that selling clothes on Vinted would end with a court claim to recover almost £6,000.She started trading on the platform to earn an income while managing Crohn's disease and caring for her four-year-old daughter.But when she became a professional seller in March, she was unable to complete Vinted's verification process, leaving thousands of pounds inaccessible in her Vinted wallet. After several weeks of trying to resolve the issue, Mali took legal action. Vinted says sellers may be asked to complete verification checks to comply with legal and regulatory requirements and 98% of transactions are completed smoothly without needing help from its support team.Vinted is hugely popular in the UK with 17 million users. The online marketplace does not charge a fee to sellers for listing on there.After the BBC reported on users whose accounts had been suspended or banned, dozens of people got in touch describing difficulties accessing money held in their Vinted wallets.Mali joined Vinted in 2024 as a side-hustle. Demand for her second-hand gymwear grew rapidly and, within months, she had set up a limited company to expand the business.This year she signed up for a Vinted Pro seller account - designed for people who want to sell a high volume of items and who are registered as a business.Within weeks she had generated almost £6,000 in sales. But when she tried to withdraw the money, she discovered her account had been restricted and was told she needed to complete a verification process."I thought, 'That's OK. It's not rocket science,'" she says. "I'd set up the business with the help of an accountant and had all the information they needed."Mali says she spotted an error Vinted had made with her name and she flagged it with Vinted, but "again nothing was done and the verification kept failing". She found herself stuck in a cycle of automated responses.  In an effort to break the deadlock, she also contacted Mangopay, the payments company that at the time operated Vinted sellers' wallets and processed transactions on the platform. She was directed back to Vinted.After eight weeks without access to the money, Mali decided to take both companies to the small claims court, spending £455 in court fees.Three days after the court claim was filed, Mali says the account was "magically verified" and she could withdraw the funds.She still pressed ahead with the case though to try to recover her court fees, costs and interest. In June, she obtained a default judgement after neither Vinted nor Mangopay responded to her claim, with the court ordering the companies to pay £1,207.50.But she has yet to receive the money. She has since been informed that Vinted and Mangopay have applied to have the judgement set aside, with a hearing scheduled for December."It's been ridiculous and incredibly stressful," she says."I need that cash. I will fight it. I'm going to tell the court their system is completely broken. I needed help and nobody helped me."Vinted said: "Ms Osmelak's check was not successful because her documents did not match the name on her Vinted account. We have since helped her update it, and her account is now verified."The company did not respond to the BBC's questions about the legal action Mali has taken and continues to pursue.Mangopay said it was "bound to professional secrecy and data protection obligations. We are, therefore, not allowed to comment on individual cases involving our clients or their users, nor can we share details about specific accounts, transactions or legal matters."

schema.headline: I took Vinted to court to get my money back

title: Copper wire upgrade caused nationwide flight chaos, US transport secretary says
description: A nationwide US ground stop that caused thousands of flight cancellations was caused by an issue following a copper wire upgrade, Transport Secretary
body: A nationwide US ground stop that caused thousands of flight cancellations was caused by an issue following a copper wire upgrade, Transport Secretary Sean Duffy said.Duffy told a news conference that the government was trying to find out whether the problem was caused by "incompetence" on the part of the company doing the upgrades, or faulty equipment.The US government does not believe it was as a result of a cyber-attack, although an investigation is still under way, Duffy said.Friday's suspension was the longest such incident since the 11 September 2001 attacks on the US and the disruption is expected to last for days.Maintenance was being carried out to switch from copper wire to fibre by a contractor called L3Harris, a technology provider company, Duffy said.The US has "an incredibly old telecommunications system", he added."It was such an old wire that it was being discontinued," he said.The transport secretary explained that a router that was being worked on had started flooding other air traffic control systems and created communication issues with planes which led the government to shut down the airspace for safety reasons.Bryan Bedford, who heads the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), told the same news conference: "We see zero evidence of anything nefarious, and zero evidence of anything AI related."On Saturday L3Harris said it had completed over 70% of the work to modernise communications infrastructure before the shutdown."We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the 13 November ground stop of our nation's air travel," it said in a statement."L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travellers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously."No flights were allowed to take off from the continental US for more than four hours from 15:54 EST (19:54 GMT) on Friday.More than 3,500 flights were cancelled and more than 2,000 delayed in the US on Saturday, according to tracking website Flight Aware, as knock-on disruption continues.In some cases, passengers were left stuck inside planes on the tarmac, unable to take off or to return to the gates. Some international flights were allowed to depart US airports, in an apparent effort to clear space.Duffy warned that a similar issue could arise again unless the US Congress approved upgrades to air traffic control infrastructure.US President Donald Trump has requested $30.1bn for the upgrades. Both chambers of Congress are currently controlled by the Republican Party.Former TSA Administrator John Pistole told the BBC that "the fact that they were able to get it restarted in four-and-a-half hours is good news - it shows a resilience in the system - but what's to say it's not going to happen tomorrow?"A nationwide ground stop has only been ordered one other time since all flights were banned from take-off for several days following the 11 September 2001 attacks.

schema.headline: Copper wire upgrade caused nationwide flight chaos, US transport secretary says

title: Noel Fielding 'appalled' by jokes he made with Russell Brand
description: Noel Fielding has said he is "appalled" by jokes he made alongside Russell Brand when the pair appeared together on TV and at live shows.The Great Bri
body: Noel Fielding has said he is "appalled" by jokes he made alongside Russell Brand when the pair appeared together on TV and at live shows.The Great British Bake Off presenter said in a statement to the Sun he was "horrified and deeply disturbed" to learn of Brand's crimes, after the disgraced comedian was jailed for rape and sexual assault.Footage of Fielding and Brand joking about rape with TV presenter Jonathan Ross on an episode of Channel 4's Big Fat Quiz of the Year in 2007 has resurfaced in the aftermath of Brand's conviction.Fielding described "some of the jokes" he made as "horrible and inappropriate", and said he had not been in contact with Brand "for many years"."I was horrified and deeply disturbed to learn of Russell Brand's crimes, which I was completely unaware of until they became public knowledge. My thoughts are with the women whose courage brought him to justice," Fielding said."I appeared on TV, radio and live charity shows with him, and whilst we played it up for the cameras and in the media, I considered it a professional relationship, rather than a personal one. I have had no contact with him for many years."Looking back at some of the jokes I made alongside him I was appalled. They were horrible and inappropriate, and I very much regret them."Ross has also released a statement distancing himself from the remarks, saying that his "thoughts are with the many, many women who have bravely come forward."Among the resurfaced footage is a clip of Brand and Fielding laughing on an episode of The Russell Brand Show, which aired on BBC Radio 2 in 2007. In it, Brand joked about kissing and holding an underage grasshopper. "How do you even know if it's a child or an adult? You don't even care, do you," Fielding responded.Brand can be heard replying: "It's a mistake I've made. I've had a lot of problems in the past, because I thought a grasshopper was above age. Before I know it, I'm in it, right, I'm kissing it, I'm holding it. Then it turns around and looks at me with onyx eyes and says: 'I'm 12.'"Brand and Fielding also performed charity gigs together as The Goth Detectives.

schema.headline: Noel Fielding 'appalled' by jokes he made with Russell Brand

title: US has floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for Nato membership, Zelensky says
description: US negotiators have touted the idea of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for Nato membership, Volody
body: US negotiators have touted the idea of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for Nato membership, Volodymyr Zelensky has said.The Ukrainian president's comments come after US President Donald Trump's envoys met Russian President Vladimir Putin and Zelensky as part of US efforts to end the war between Russia and Ukraine.Kyiv has long sought membership of the military alliance, but this has previously been opposed by the US and others while Russia has said another Nato member on its border is unacceptable.Russia controls most of the industrial region of Donbas and Zelensky has consistently said Ukraine is unwilling to give up sovereign territory.Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022."The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins Nato? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?' This was the first time this had been raised," Zelensky said in remarks released by his office on Saturday.He went on to say that if he received a specific proposal that contained security guarantees, no constraints on Ukraine's military and funds to rebuild the country, he would put it to a referendum.US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff travelled to the Irish capital, Dublin, on Thursday to meet Zelensky, after a round of talks with Putin in Moscow.Comments by both Putin and Kremlin officials suggest that Russia's position on the war has not shifted. It has previously proposed limits on the size of Ukraine's military, territorial concessions and Kyiv's guaranteed neutrality as conditions of a peace deal.Ukraine has rejected these, arguing that such constraints would hamper its ability to stave off any future invasion.It is not clear the US is actually proposing Nato membership – the White House has not yet replied to a request for comment and it is understood that Ukraine itself sees that as unrealistic.Other Nato members are wary and the Kremlin has always been fiercely opposed. It is one reason why Russia started this war in the first place.It is possible the American envoys were exploring Ukraine's "red lines" when it comes to occupied land in the Donbas. Zelensky said recently that the US mediators believed Kyiv only had to cede territory to achieve peace and were applying pressure, keen to do a deal as soon as possible.Ukraine is sure that Russia's ambitions are far greater and has long seen Nato as its only sure protection.So it is also possible that Zelensky made this suggestion public in order to re-open a discussion that had been considered all-but closed.He maintains that the idea is now "back on the agenda" as part of an "extremely difficult conversation" on European security.It also looks like Ukrainian push-back against Russia's renewed hardline stance. Moscow now talks about a "new European security architecture", which is long-standing Russian code for a weaker Nato.The issue appears to have been the main focus at the latest round of talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US in Abu Dhabi this week.Russia has insisted again that it will not agree to cease fighting until a final peace deal is in place that would include handing over territories its troops have not captured, in addition to the Crimean peninsula it annexed illegally in 2014.Russia currently occupies roughly a fifth of Ukrainian territory, including most of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions that compose the Donbas. The latest round of talks come after a period of fraught relations between Kyiv and Washington over Ukrainian strikes on oil facilities deep inside Russia, which Trump had asked Ukraine to pause to facilitate the supply of Russian diesel to ease global fuel prices.Zelensky then accused US officials of limiting Ukraine's Starlink internet service, which it uses to co-ordinate defensive operations, while Trump said it was "time for Ukraine to get a new president" and called for fresh elections.Elections are suspended while Ukraine remains under martial law, but Zelensky has previously said he was willing to hold them within months of a peace deal being reached and would give up the presidency in exchange for Nato membership.

schema.headline: US has floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for Nato membership, Zelensky says

title: Young people should have legal guarantee of job or training, Milburn tells BBC
description: Young people should have a legal guarantee of a job, training or employment support, the author of a major review of youth unemployment has told the B
body: Young people should have a legal guarantee of a job, training or employment support, the author of a major review of youth unemployment has told the BBC.Alan Milburn, the former Labour minister whose proposals on welfare and young people will be unveiled on Tuesday, said those who refuse to take up the help could lose their benefits.In an interview to be broadcast on Sunday, Milburn called for a radical shift in government spending away from benefits for young people to measures that support them into work.He claims the government spends 25 times as much on benefits for young people than it spends on supporting them into employment, and believes the ratio should shift to two to one.That would mean significant cuts to benefit spending and significant extra taxpayers' cash for training, education or other forms of support.Milburn said "the pendulum's swung far too far from the one to the other - £25 to one, and we can take everything to £2 to one".He added: "To do that, we've got to invest, less in benefits, so we've got to be paying out less in benefits."The former MP acknowledged that would mean some young people losing out on benefits, arguing the system should focus on helping people into work rather than keeping them dependent on welfare.Milburn said the government is already spending £22bn a year supporting young people who are economically inactive, and that money needs to be spent differently. He has already said that the under 25s should no longer be able to claim some health benefits – the personal independence payment and the health element of Universal Credit.In his other major announcement, Milburn spoke of the proposal he calls an "opportunity guarantee" for young people.This would put a legal duty on government to ensure young people have access to a route into employment.He said: "It should be a guarantee for a young person. Because at the moment the only guarantee they've got is a very simple thing. To get a benefit. What sort of life is that?"The "opportunity guarantee" might work similarly to the way that councils have a legal responsibility to offer homeless people accommodation or advice, or accommodate children in care.Milburn argues previous employment schemes have been temporary, and says a permanent legal entitlement is needed to tackle the long-running problem of young people not in education, employment or training.The government is expected broadly to welcome the proposals, which will be published in full on Tuesday, with a statement in Parliament and draft laws early next year.Almost one million young people in the UK are not in employment, education or training - otherwise known as Neet - according to the latest data from the Office for National Statistics.Prime Minister Andy Burnham has described Milburn's forthcoming report as a "watershed moment," but stopped short of committing to implementing its recommendations in full.Burnham also insisted paying for the reforms would not mean "more money" but "spending differently" in government when pressed on the large upfront investment they are expected to require.Asked whether he would accept the politically sensitive report in full, Burnham declined to provide that "blanket assurance".Speaking at the Welsh Labour conference on Saturday, Burnham said that the report addressed the "youth detachment" that has been on the rise since the pandemic. "It can't be right that we've stripped away support from young people as a society, as life is getting harder for them and growing up is getting more difficult," he said.The prime minister added that the government was also looking at a new vision for schooling that is "not focused solely on the university route" and which offers technical education alongside traditional academic learning. Lord Blunkett, a former Labour home secretary, told the BBC that money from cutting benefits spending should be reassigned to supporting employment "at least in the immediate future".Speaking on Radio 4's Today programme, he said reforms should focus on "transferring resource that currently goes into paying for failure, keeping youngsters at home, isolated, lonely, into actually putting the money in and the resource and the commitment in to making those jobs available".Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch has previously said the government should not be spending "lots of time" on employment schemes, which she said would ultimately fail.Her party and Reform UK have argued for significant cuts to welfare, including to fund a boost to defence.Reform economy spokesman Robert Jenrick said: "This review is pointless unless we get action from Burnham straight away. "It cannot be right that this continues for another 10 years before the youth benefits bill comes down."Green Party leader Zack Polanski said it was "disappointing" the Milburn review had "come up with the same tired conclusions" on youth unemployment.Polanski added: "Using benefit sanctions to force young people into low-paid, insecure work doesn't solve the structural inequalities they face, and it deepens poverty."The Liberal Democrats want the government to introduce a 100-hour work experience guarantee and a careers coach for every young person.They believe this would equip youngsters with the best possible skills before they leave school.The TUC - the umbrella group for unions in the UK - welcomed Milburn's proposal of a legal guarantee as a "game changer", describing the country's number of Neets as a "national emergency".But it stressed that funding for additional support for young people should not come from public service budgets. "In further education, funding needs to be targeted at the workforce, as well as provision, to tackle the recruitment and retention crisis and massive pay disparities in the sector," it said."A zero sum approach would be wrong and counter-productive."

schema.headline: Young people should have legal guarantee of job or training, Milburn tells BBC

title: Eurovision Asia: Philippines wins continent's first song contest
description: Figure caption, Philippines' Carmelle has won the first Eurovision Song Contest Asia with her women's empowerment anthem Sobra-SobraByJonathan HeadSou
body: Figure caption, Philippines' Carmelle has won the first Eurovision Song Contest Asia with her women's empowerment anthem Sobra-SobraByJonathan HeadSouth East Asia correspondent, in BangkokThuong LeReporting fromBangkok and Jack GreyBBC NewsUpdated 1 hour agoThe Philippines have won the very first Eurovision Song Contest Asia, hosted in Bangkok and with 11 countries vying for the title.Nineteen-year-old singer Carmelle was always a front runner with her women's empowerment anthem Sobra-Sobra, complete with its catchy rap section.She earned 211 points in total - 93 from the jury and 118 from the public vote - ahead of Thailand's MANG x DAOU in second place with 170 points.There was a joyous atmosphere at the One Bangkok Arena as the crowd cheered the contestants and celebrated the popular winner.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Carmelle was the youngest contestant in the comeptions at 19 years old Carmelle, the youngest contestant in the competition, was an obvious favourite with the juries and the public despite strong showings from several nations. Other notable acts included MANG x DAOU, whose emotive duet Aroma elicited huge cheers from the home crowd.Bangladeshi beatboxers Beatmosphere eschewed the traditional backing track, instead using their voices to replicate the sounds of drums and basslines.And Laos's Thinla performed her crowd-pleasing song Bae in a traditional Lao hilltribe outfit.However, the Laotian song had a unintentional second outing after the music video was played over an apparent technical issue during the broadcast - meaning it was the last song the audience heard before the vote. Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Thinla wore a traditional Lao hilltribe outfit during her performanceThe voting system worked much the same as the European Eurovison, with the public vote accounting for 50% of the result and the other 50% coming from the 11 national juries - with additional points awarded from a rest of the world vote. Here's how the final scoreboard ended: 1. The Philippines - 211 points2. Thailand - 170 points3. Vietnam - 164 points4. Malaysia - 152 points5. Laos - 139 points6. Bhutan - 126 points7. Republic of Korea - 113 points8. Mongolia - 94 points9. Nepal - 69 points10. Cambodia - 61 points11. Bangladesh - 35 pointsAlso performing during the broadcast was 2026 Eurovision Song Contest winner Dara from Bulgaria, who performed her winning song Bangaranga and new song Bad Idea.Thai superstar Jeff Satur also made an appearance, hitting the high notes in his performance of Black Tie.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Vietnam's Toc Tien came third with 164 pointsEurovision in Asia was an idea that has been talked about for decades, but one that never seemed to materialise - despite many false starts - until now. There is a huge enthusiasm here for Eurovision Asia, but a large number of the audience were established fans of the original contest from other countries and regions of the world.Speaking after the show, fan Zelie Pereira - who travelled from Scotland to Thailand to attend - said she was "very happy" with Carmelle's win.Image source, BBC/Jack TranImage caption, Eurvosion superfans Michael, Scarlett and Zelie travelled from the UK to Thailand to watch Eurovision Asia's first outingKorea, Vietnam and Laos also received praise from Pereira and her friends Michael Peters and Scarlett Massie, both from England."It was amazing, a very high standard," said Massie."The dance was amazing. The sets were amazing. The costumes were amazing. The singing was amazing. Incredible", Peters added.They confidently declared that "Asia Vision" should be the name for next year's show.For some, it seems the excitement for another edition is already building.However the crowd at the One Bangkok Arena thinned out not long after the Philippines singer Carmelle lifted the trophy.The arena was crowded, but not full, and it's still not clear how much commitment there is among regional broadcasters to keep the contest going and expand it to more than 11 countries.

schema.headline: Eurovision Asia: Philippines wins continent's first song contest

title: Nvidia: How the Jensen Huang scandal exposed a headache for business-friendly Singapore
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByTessa Wong and Osmond ChiaReporting fromSingaporeA major scandal involving Nvidia founder Jensen Huang and a suspected Chi
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByTessa Wong and Osmond ChiaReporting fromSingaporeA major scandal involving Nvidia founder Jensen Huang and a suspected Chinese spy based in Singapore has cast a spotlight on the city-state's success as a global chip hub - and a location for alleged illicit trade.On Thursday, Huang stepped down from the US chip giant after admitting he had an affair. He was reportedly involved with a woman named Alice Huang, who ran Singaporean data centre company Megaspeed, a major buyer of Nvidia's chips.For decades, Singapore has painstakingly cultivated a reputation as an open, business-friendly economy offering easy access to both the US and Chinese markets.With the AI boom, it has become a major hub for the trade of high-end semiconductor chips in recent years.Singapore was the second-largest billing centre globally last year for Nvidia, accounting for nearly a fifth of what the US chip giant earns.But notably, less than 1% of its earnings were for chips that actually entered Singapore, as the island acts as a hub for many Asian companies to place orders and send them elsewhere.Since 2022, when the US restricted advanced American semiconductors from being exported to China or acquired by Chinese companies, US officials have been concerned that other countries such as Singapore could be used by Chinese companies to gain access to the chips.Megaspeed is a case in point.It became the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in South East Asia and is suspected of giving backdoor access to these chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.Singapore has said that while it does not enforce "unilateral export controls imposed by other countries" it expects all companies in its jurisdiction to respect such regulations.The city-state has had some success in policing this.It has charged four companies and five individuals - including Chinese nationals - for various offences including fraud, following US concerns that Chinese AI company DeepSeek had been buying Nvidia chips from third parties in Singapore, among other places.They also tried to probe Megaspeed, but were faced with a number of difficulties.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Megaspeed's office in Singapore In a statement released on Thursday, the government said that since February 2025, they had been looking into whether Megaspeed and other firms had made false declarations about data servers which were purchased and exported through Singapore.The companies stated the equipment would end up in neighbouring Malaysia, but Singapore authorities suspect the equipment's final destinations were elsewhere.Singapore said it sought assistance from US authorities several times to get more information from one of the investigated companies - Supermicro, a US-based company which the BBC understands was supplying computer servers to Megaspeed.But "despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance", it said in its statement. The BBC has sought comment from the US State Department.Singapore authorities said they had also investigated Alice Huang - not for espionage, but for any possible role in Megaspeed's suspected fraud. In the end, they found "insufficient evidence" of crime and let her leave Singapore in February this year, after holding her passport for several months.Since launching their probe nearly two years ago, Singapore has yet to bring any charges against Megaspeed or any of the companies and individuals linked to the case.Singapore and US investigations into Megaspeed are still ongoing.In 2024, US officials had paid a visit to a Malaysian data centre owned by Megaspeed and saw Nvidia technology still in their boxes, raising concerns that Megaspeed was shipping high-end chips out elsewhere, according to a report by the New York Times.Last year, Megaspeed appeared to have imported 50,000 more chips than Nvidia could account for, according to a Bloomberg report. Nvidia later adjusted its own figures after visiting more warehouses.Megaspeed has maintained it has always acted lawfully and that previous inspections by authorities found no evidence of illegal activity. On Thursday, the company said it "welcomes appropriate government scrutiny" and that it is "committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government".China has also long refuted accusations that its companies and institutions are illegally obtaining high-end US chips.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia on Thursday following a board meetingHow Megaspeed and Alice Huang came to Singapore highlights other vulnerabilities stemming from the city-state's openness.In recent years, the city-state has become a prime destination for Chinese companies, with tech firms such as TikTok and Manus making it their global headquarters. Besides Singapore's ease of doing business, it has a population that is mostly ethnically Chinese and largely views China positively.For a Chinese firm, Singapore offers a base near the mainland and a "neutral address" that global customers and investors accept, said Winston Ma, adjunct professor at New York University's School of Law.But critics say this has given rise to "Singapore-washing", where Chinese companies use the city-state's clean image to obscure their origins, reduce suspicions and even cover up dubious activities.Washington-based security analysis group C4ADS told the BBC they had assessed Alice Huang's setup of Megaspeed to be such a case.BBC checks of corporate records in China, Hong Kong and Singapore found that in 2019, Huang sold a gaming company and its subsidiaries to Chinese gaming firm 7Road.In March 2023, a 7Road subsidiary in Singapore named Huang as its executive director. The next day it changed its name - to Megaspeed.Huang was in charge for eight months before she transferred the company to a Singaporean man. During this period, Megaspeed went through "a critical period of corporate restructuring and regional expansion", and her corporate relationships raised questions about whether "Megaspeed's Singaporean identity is genuine or effectively Chinese-controlled", according to C4ADS.Even after she transferred Megaspeed, C4ADS assessed that she was still "practically in control" of the company, based on her links to Megaspeed via another company as well as LinkedIn posts where she continued to identify herself as Megaspeed's "chairwoman" at conferences.Megaspeed has not answered BBC queries regarding the company's and Alice Huang's links to China and the Chinese government.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Alice Huang, seen here in Taipei with Jensen Huang last year, ran Megaspeed for several months in 2023All this reinforces the dilemma faced by Singapore."For the longest time, Singapore has managed to enjoy the best of both worlds with excellent relations with US and China," Nanyang Technological University politics and international studies lecturer Dylan Loh said.Singapore has long positioned itself as a neutral party between the two superpowers. Its prime minister Lawrence Wong has insisted that his country is neither pro-China nor pro-America, but "pro-Singapore".But Loh says this balancing act "has now fast become very difficult to manage and sometimes quite fraught too" with the US-China dispute over chips.With the Megaspeed case, the tightrope Singapore has walked is set to get even narrower, according to analysts.Beijing may ask why Singapore is investigating issues pertaining to US restrictions and whether they are siding with the US' interests, says Chong Ja Ian, a Singaporean political scientist and non-resident scholar with Carnegie China.Washington, in turn, might read Singapore's latest statement as "pushing blame" on the US, which could lead to backlash from the White House, he said."Singapore has made a policy position not to take sides. But by not choosing a side, they run the risk of being seen as complicit" in either side's agenda, he said.But Benjamin Ho, an assistant professor and China expert at Singapore's S Rajaratnam School of International Studies, noted that this was "not the first or last time Singapore will be caught between the US and China"."This is the price that an open economy has to grapple with - you get caught in the middle when things turn sour."Additional reporting by Jack Lau of the BBC's Global China Unit.

schema.headline: Nvidia: How the Jensen Huang scandal exposed a headache for business-friendly Singapore

title: Thousands turn out in Edinburgh to protest against AI data centres
description: Image source, Press AssociationImage caption, Protesters marched down the Royal Mile towards the Scottish Parliament ByMary McCoolBBC Scotland NewsUpd
body: Image source, Press AssociationImage caption, Protesters marched down the Royal Mile towards the Scottish Parliament ByMary McCoolBBC Scotland NewsUpdated 2 hours agoThousands of people have joined a protest in Edinburgh against the building of large-scale AI data centres.Demonstrators with placards - and some dressed in costume - assembled at the top of the Royal Mile before marching towards the Scottish Parliament.The event comes at a time of widespread debate about the environmental impact of data centres and is part of a wave of protests across Europe.The Scottish government will soon publish new planning guidance on data centres and said it was developing a strategy to maximise the "public benefit".Image source, Getty ImagesImage source, Press AssociationImage caption, Some demonstrators attended in eye-catching costume to draw attention to particular issuesImage source, Press AssociationInnovation Minister Alyn Smith recently said data centres were "the whisky bonds of the AI sector".However protesters made it clear they disagree - carrying slogans such as "AI data centres threaten humanity" and "AI data centres: costing the Earth".Some attended to voice their opposition to plans for data centres in particular communities - including Cockenzie, East Lothian, and Larbert, Falkirk.Kim Cairns, a campaigner for 'Say No To Chapelcross AI Data Centre', told BBC Scotland News her community was worried about noise, road closures and access problems during the construction phase.She was also concerned about the noise the centre would generate when it was operational.Kim said: "It's not going to enrich anybody's lives. For Chapelcross it's the sheer size of it, the amount of electricity it's going to need."At the moment it's green fields with sheep and cows in it. It's going to be a monstrosity on the environment. "The air pollution, the light pollution - it's just not needed."Image source, Press AssociationImage source, Press AssociationAI is seen by some as the most transformative technology ever made but others have warned there is chance that if the frightening pace of development continues it "could kill all humans" within the next decade.Meanwhile, Scotland's data centre debate centres around the scale and impact of the sites themselves.At the moment, the biggest data centre in Scotland is thought to be DataVita's site in Airdrie, North Lanarkshire, which has a capacity for 12MW.But if one planned for Chapelcross, Dumfries and Galloway, goes ahead it will have a capacity of 1,000MW - making it one of the largest data centres in the world.The Scottish Greens and campaign groups have called for a moratorium on large data centres, arguing they could undermine climate targets and place additional pressure on renewable energy supplies.The innovation minister previously told BBC Scotland some of the discourse around the subject was "wild".Smith said: "You'd think there wasn't a planning system at all. "Comparing a really bad data centre in the middle of the Utah desert doesn't track through to what we're going to have in Scotland."Figure caption, Thousands turn out in Edinburgh to protest against AI data centresFriends of the Earth campaigner Kim Pratt believes the people of Scotland should have the final say on the building of data centres.She said: "The way that these data centres are being proposed is going to make a lot of profit for big tech companies but they're going to have huge impacts for people in Scotland."These developments are so massive they're going to have national-level impacts -they're energy hungry developments. "There would be a massive increase in our energy bills but also in terms of climate impact as well."The Scottish government is only taking a few months to consider these impacts - and these developments are so new, we don't know what all the impacts will be."Scotcast: AI and data centres: what now?15 SeptemberThe Scottish government confirmed it would publish new planning guidance on data centres before the end of the year and was "developing a strategic approach to maximising the public benefit from data centres located in Scotland".A spokesperson added: "Planning authorities are also now required to notify ministers of new data centre applications, with a new planning direction also mandating an Environmental Impact Assessment to be submitted during planning for all new data centres with a power capacity exceeding 50 megawatts."

schema.headline: Thousands turn out in Edinburgh to protest against AI data centres
